cues.text: Let us finish the course with a section that brings everything together: Final consolidation.
Up to now, you have met several separate ideas.
This closing section asks you to see them as one connected chain of reasoning.
The six ideas to connect are these: digital strategy, disruption diagnosis, innovation framework selection, roadmap sequencing, platform ecosystem economics, and governance.
Let us walk through them in that order, and see how each one leads to the next.
First, digital strategy.
This is the starting point.
Digital strategy sets out how an organisation intends to use digital technologies and capabilities to create value and compete.
It tells you where the organisation wants to go, and why.
Without it, technology choices are scattered and have no clear purpose.
Second, disruption diagnosis.
Once you know your strategic direction, you need to understand the forces acting on you.

Disruption diagnosis means examining how the market, the technology, customer behaviour and new competitors are changing the environment, and judging how serious the threat or opportunity is for your particular organisation.
Strategy without diagnosis is guesswork, because you would not know what you are responding to.
Third, innovation framework selection.
After diagnosis, you choose a suitable framework to guide the innovation response.
Different situations call for different frameworks, so the skill here is matching the framework to the problem in front of you, rather than applying one favourite model to everything.
Fourth, roadmap sequencing.
A framework tells you how to think; a roadmap tells you what to do, and in what order.
Sequencing means deciding which initiatives come first, which depend on others, and how they build on one another over time.
Poor sequencing is a common reason that good ideas fail in practice.
Fifth, platform ecosystem economics.
Many digital businesses create value through platforms and ecosystems, where several parties, such as customers, producers and partners, interact and benefit from one another.
Economics here means understanding how value is created, how it is shared among participants, and how the platform sustains itself financially.
Sixth, governance.
Governance is the set of decision rights, rules, responsibilities and oversight that keep all of this accountable and under control.
It makes sure that strategy, innovation, roadmap and platform decisions are made properly, by the right people, with appropriate checks.

So the whole chain runs like this: strategy gives direction; diagnosis explains the pressure; framework selection chooses the method; the roadmap sequences the action; platform economics explains how value is created and shared; and governance keeps it all accountable.
If one link is missing, the others weaken.
Now to the second requirement in this section.
You must be able to distinguish frameworks in scenarios.
This means that when you are given a short business situation, you should be able to recognise which framework fits it, and explain why, rather than simply recalling definitions.
Read the scenario carefully, identify what is actually changing and what problem is being solved, and then match the framework to that need.
You must also be able to identify whether a change is product, process, organisational or business-model innovation.
Let us take these four types in turn, with a simple test for each.
Product innovation is a change in what the organisation offers.
The test is: has the thing being sold or delivered to the customer changed?
A new or significantly improved product or service is product innovation.
Process innovation is a change in how the organisation produces or delivers what it offers.
The test is: has the way the work is done changed, even though the offering looks the same to the customer?
Faster, cheaper or more reliable internal methods are process innovation.
Organisational innovation is a change in how the organisation is structured and managed.
The test is: have roles, teams, decision-making, culture or ways of working changed?
Examples include new reporting structures or new collaboration practices.
Business-model innovation is a change in how the organisation creates, delivers and captures value as a whole.
The test is: has the logic of earning revenue changed, for example who pays, what they pay for, or how value reaches them?
When you face a scenario, ask these questions in sequence.
What is the customer receiving?
That points to product.
How is the work being done?
That points to process.
How are people structured and managed?
That points to organisational.
How does the organisation make money and deliver value overall?
That points to business model.
Be careful, because a single initiative can touch more than one type.
When that happens, identify the primary change, the one that is driving the others, and explain the secondary effects separately.
To close, remember the two skills this section asks for.
First, connect the chain: strategy, diagnosis, framework, roadmap, platform economics and governance.
Second, classify with confidence: product, process, organisational or business-model innovation, and distinguish frameworks when a scenario is put in front of you.
